title: Duel on the riverbank
translation: At a place called Shukugawara, a crowd of boroboro, wandering beggar monks, had gathered to chant the Buddha's name. Another boroboro came in from outside and asked: "Excuse me, is there a boro here by the name of Irooshi?"
Someone in the crowd answered: "Irooshi is here. Who's asking?"
"My name is Shira Bonji. I've heard that my teacher, a man called so-and-so, was killed in the east by a boro called Irooshi. I'd like to meet that man and settle the score. That's why I'm asking."

"Good of you to come looking for me," said Irooshi. "Yes, that happened. But if we fight here, we'll defile the hall. Let's meet on the riverbank out front. And please, all of you, don't help either side. If a lot of people get hurt, it'll get in the way of the service."
With that settled, the two of them went out to the riverbank, ran each other through to their hearts' content, and both died.

I don't think there were any boroboro in the old days. Apparently they started not long ago with people who called themselves boronji, bonji or kanji. They look as if they've left the world behind, but they can't let go of themselves. They look as if they want to follow the Buddha, but what they actually do is fight. They live without restraint and without shame. Still, they think nothing of dying and don't hesitate for a second, and that struck me as clean. So I've written it down just as it was told to me.

literal: At a place called Shukugawara, many boroboro had gathered and were chanting the nine-grade nembutsu, when
a boroboro coming in from outside asked, 'Perhaps among you there is a boro called the monk Irooshi?', and
from among them (someone) answered, 'Irooshi is here. Who is it that says so?', and

(the other) said, 'I am one called Shira Bonji. I heard that my teacher, a person called so-and-so, was killed in the eastern provinces by a boro called Irooshi, so I thought I would like to meet that person and take my revenge, and I am asking for him.'

Irooshi said, 'It is admirable that you have come looking. That did happen. If I meet you here, it will defile the place of practice. Let us meet at the riverbank in front. I beg you: you companions, do not help either side. If it becomes trouble for many people, it will hinder the Buddhist service.' Having settled this,
the two went out to the riverbank and met, pierced each other to their hearts' content, and both died.
Were there no such things as boroboro in the old days?
In recent times, those who were called boronji, bonji, kanji and the like were, it is said, their beginning.
They seem to have abandoned the world, but their attachment to self is deep; they seem to wish for the Buddha's way, but they make fighting their business.
Their way of life is heedless and shameless, but the side of them that takes death lightly and does not hesitate at all seemed clean to me, and I write it down just as a person told it.

notes.text: Where this was is not certain. The 1925 edition mentions two theories, one in Settsu (near Osaka) and one in Musashi; the second is usually taken to be Shukugawara by the Tama River, in today's Kawasaki.

Wandering mendicants of Kenkō's time, half monk, half vagrant, also called ぼろ for short. They are often seen as forerunners of the {虚無僧|こむそう} of the Edo period, the begging monks with the basket hats and bamboo flutes.

{念仏|ねんぶつ}: chanting the name of the Buddha Amida. {九品|くほん}: the nine levels of rebirth in Amida's Pure Land. A {九品|くほん}の{念仏|ねんぶつ} was a chanting service connected with those nine levels; the 1925 edition explains it as a nembutsu chanted in nine changing melodies.

notes.quote: 殺されけりと承りしかば
notes.text: Two past auxiliaries side by side. けり: the killing is something Shira Bonji only heard about. き (しか): the hearing is something he experienced himself. Irooshi answers with き too, さる{事|こと}はべりき: 'that did happen', he was there.

notes.quote: 道場をけがし侍るべし
notes.text: {道場|だうぢやう}: a place of Buddhist practice, here the hall where they were chanting. Blood and death would pollute it. Irooshi is careful about the hall and the service, and not at all careful about himself.
The people standing by, the companions of either man. {見|み}つぐ: 'to back someone up, to help'.

notes.quote: 心ゆくばかりに貫きあひて
notes.text: {心|こころ}ゆく: 'to one's heart's content'. The killing is told in one flat clause, without a word of comment.
Names that early mendicants of this kind called themselves. ぼろぼろ probably comes from ぼろんじ. Kenkō hedges twice here, with にや and とかや: he is not sure where they came from.
Two Buddhist terms. {放逸|はういつ}: heedless, without discipline. {無慚|むざん}: without shame. Kenkō condemns them in Buddhist words and then praises them anyway, for one thing.
いさぎよし: 'clean, pure, unhesitating'. Modern {潔|いさぎよ}い, used for someone who accepts defeat or death without fuss, is the same word.
